blocks.text: 1. Gradient Descent

blocks.alt: A current point uses the gradient to step downhill
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439733078-517973305.png

Backpropagation, already covered earlier in this module, computes exactly how much the loss would change for a tiny nudge to any given weight. Gradient Descent is the general algorithm that actually uses those computed gradients to adjust the weights themselves.

Backpropagation computes the gradients; Gradient Descent decides what to actually do with them, a genuinely important, clean division of labor between these two closely related, but genuinely distinct, concepts covered throughout this module.
2. The Core Idea

blocks.alt: Starting high on the loss surface, stepping downhill reaches low loss
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439733079-410271399.png

This connects back to the ball-rolling-downhill intuition, already introduced in the Momentum topic. At every single step, Gradient Descent moves each weight slightly in the direction that actually reduces the loss.

The gradient itself points toward increasing loss, so weights genuinely move in the exact opposite direction, the direct, foundational mechanism behind essentially every optimizer covered throughout this entire module.
3. The Update Rule

blocks.alt: The current weight minus the learning rate times gradient gives the new weight
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439733079-178536385.png
The update rule itself is genuinely simple: take the current weight value, then subtract the learning rate multiplied by the gradient, producing the new, updated weight value.

This exact process repeats across every single weight in the network, every single step of training, the fundamental, repeated computation underlying essentially all of Deep Learning training covered throughout this course.

blocks.text: 4. Choosing the Learning Rate

blocks.alt: Too small a learning rate gives slow progress while too large overshoots the minimum
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439733328-564879993.png

This connects back to the learning rate, a genuinely central hyperparameter throughout this entire module. Too large a learning rate causes steps to overshoot, and the loss can genuinely bounce around unpredictably, or even increase, rather than steadily decreasing.

Too small a learning rate instead causes genuinely slow, overly cautious progress toward the actual minimum, wasting considerable training time taking unnecessarily tiny steps, exactly the tension Learning Rate Scheduling, already covered later in this module, was specifically built to address.
5. The Local Minima Challenge

blocks.alt: A local minimum is compared against the global minimum
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439733329-539062167.png

A genuine, real challenge on complex loss surfaces is the local minimum, a point that looks like the bottom of a valley from its immediate surroundings, but is not actually the true, global lowest point across the entire loss surface.

Gradient Descent can genuinely get stuck here, since the gradient at a local minimum is exactly zero, providing no signal at all pointing toward any genuinely better, lower point elsewhere on the surface.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: In practice, genuinely deep neural networks turn out to have surprisingly few problematic local minima relative to their enormous number of parameters, a somewhat counterintuitive but well-documented empirical finding worth knowing.

blocks.text: 6. Three Variants, Previewed

blocks.alt: Gradient descent has batch, stochastic, and mini-batch variants
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439733330-574461525.png

This connects forward to Batch, Stochastic, and Mini-Batch Gradient Descent, each covered in its own dedicated topic earlier in this module. These represent three genuinely distinct ways to actually decide how much data feeds into each individual update step.

Plain Gradient Descent, covered throughout this topic, describes the general update rule itself, while these three variants each answer the genuinely separate, practical question of exactly how much data to actually use when computing that update at each step.
7. Convex Versus Non-Convex Loss Surfaces

blocks.alt: A convex surface has one minimum while a non-convex surface has many minima
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439733331-509897692.png

This connects back to Linear Regression's own loss surface, already covered in the traditional Machine Learning course. A convex loss surface, shaped like a single, simple bowl with exactly one minimum, guarantees Gradient Descent will genuinely find that true minimum.

A genuinely non-convex loss surface, the kind neural networks actually have given their many stacked, non-linear layers, offers no such guarantee, though Gradient Descent still works remarkably well in practice regardless, a genuinely important, somewhat surprising empirical fact worth understanding.

blocks.text: 8. A Historical Foundation

Gradient Descent itself predates Deep Learning by decades, a genuinely general optimization technique used across many fields well beyond machine learning entirely, from physics to economics to engineering.

Its specific application to training neural networks is what this entire module has actually covered in depth, adapting this genuinely old, well-established mathematical idea to the specific, modern challenge of training genuinely large, deep networks.
9. Why This Foundation Genuinely Matters

Understanding plain Gradient Descent clearly matters directly before its many variants, since every optimizer covered throughout this module, Momentum through Nadam, is genuinely an enhancement to this exact core idea, not a wholly separate, unrelated algorithm.

Understanding this foundation first, covered fully throughout this topic, makes every single later enhancement genuinely make sense as a targeted, well-motivated improvement, rather than an arbitrary, disconnected collection of separate techniques with no clear, unifying thread.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Gradient Descent is the general algorithm that actually uses computed gradients to adjust weights.
At every step, it moves each weight slightly opposite to the gradient, toward decreasing loss.
The update rule subtracts the learning rate times the gradient from the current weight value.
Too large a learning rate causes overshooting; too small causes genuinely slow, cautious progress.
Gradient Descent can get stuck at a local minimum, where the gradient is exactly zero with no escape signal.
Batch, Stochastic, and Mini-Batch Gradient Descent, covered in this module, differ in how much data feeds each step.
A convex loss surface guarantees finding the true minimum; a non-convex one, like a network's, does not.
Gradient Descent predates Deep Learning by decades, a general technique used across many fields.
Every optimizer covered throughout this module, Momentum through Nadam, is genuinely an enhancement to this core idea.
